boundary_rationale: The letter opens with its sender formula, rp:1Cor.1.1 Παῦλος κλητὸς ἀπόστολος, and adds Sosthenes as co-sender. The adscript of 1:2 names the assembly of God at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus, together with those who call on the Lord's name in other places. The prescript ends with the greeting rp:1Cor.1.3 χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη. At 1:4 the speech act changes from salutation to thanks, so the seam falls after 1:3; the RP pilcrow at 1:4 stands at that seam, though the cut rests on the change of main verb.

Set aside because prescript and thanksgiving are two distinct letter forms with distinct main verbs, and keeping them apart lets the address and the thanks be weighed on their own terms.

boundary_rationale: The body opens at 1:10 with the appeal formula rp:1Cor.1.10 Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, which turns from thanks to petition and asks the readers to speak alike and be knit together in one mind. The ground follows in a report from Chloe's people, rp:1Cor.1.11 Ἐδηλώθη γάρ μοι. The party slogans of 1:12 begin rp:1Cor.1.12 Ἐγὼ μέν εἰμι Παύλου, and the questions of 1:13 and the baptism recollection of 1:14-1:16 answer them. In 1:17 Paul turns from whom he baptized to what he was sent to do, ending on rp:1Cor.1.17 ὁ σταυρὸς τοῦ χριστοῦ. The RP pilcrow at 1:10 stands at the onset, and the RP pilcrow at 1:18 stands after that turn. Confidence is moderate-to-low because 1:17 faces both ways.

boundary_rationale: With rp:1Cor.1.18 Ὁ λόγος γὰρ ὁ τοῦ σταυροῦ the subject moves from Paul's commission to the message itself, folly to those perishing and power to those being saved. A citation follows under rp:1Cor.1.19 Γέγραπται γάρ. A run of questions beginning rp:1Cor.1.20 Ποῦ σοφός presses the point, and the contrast of Jews and Greeks in 1:22-1:24 restates it. The step closes on the maxim rp:1Cor.1.25 Ὅτι τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ θεοῦ σοφώτερον, which rounds off the contrast of wisdom and folly. The RP pilcrow at 1:18 stands at the onset and the RP pilcrow at 1:26 at the close seam, where an imperative turns the argument to the readers' own calling.

boundary_rationale: The step opens with rp:1Cor.2.6 Σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις and develops one claim across its length: a hidden wisdom of God, unknown to the rulers of this age, revealed by the Spirit and discerned by the spiritual. A citation at 2:9 speaks of what eye has not seen. The answer comes in rp:1Cor.2.10 Ἡμῖν δὲ ὁ θεὸς ἀπεκάλυψεν, revelation through the Spirit. The contrast rp:1Cor.2.14 Ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος then sets the unspiritual person against the spiritual. After the question about the Lord's mind the step closes with rp:1Cor.2.16 Ἡμεῖς δὲ νοῦν χριστοῦ ἔχομεν. A Byzantine pilcrow heads 2:6 as well. At 3:1 a vocative and first-person narrative turn back to the Corinthians as people of the flesh, which closes the step.

boundary_rationale: With rp:1Cor.3.1 Καὶ ἐγώ, ἀδελφοί Paul turns from the spiritual person to the Corinthians, whom he had to address as people of the flesh, infants in Christ. The image of milk and solid food in 3:2 and the evidence of jealousy and strife in 3:3 lead back to the party slogans at 3:4. The step ends on the charge rp:1Cor.3.4 οὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐστε. At 3:5 a question about who Apollos and Paul are opens the account of the servants, so the seam falls after 3:4.

boundary_rationale: A prohibition, rp:1Cor.3.18 Μηδεὶς ἑαυτὸν ἐξαπατάτω, opens a hortatory close to the discussion of wisdom: whoever seems wise in this age should become foolish. Scripture is cited under rp:1Cor.3.19 Γέγραπται γάρ. The inference rp:1Cor.3.21 Ὥστε μηδεὶς καυχάσθω draws the consequence for boasting in leaders. The step ends rp:1Cor.3.23 ὑμεῖς δὲ χριστοῦ, χριστὸς δὲ θεοῦ. In the Byzantine text 3:18 carries a pilcrow. At 4:1 a new account of how apostles should be regarded begins.

boundary_rationale: With rp:1Cor.4.6 Ταῦτα δέ, ἀδελφοί, μετεσχημάτισα Paul explains that he has applied the images to himself and Apollos, so that the readers learn not to go beyond what is written or be puffed up. Questions at 4:7 lead into irony. It begins with rp:1Cor.4.8 Ἤδη κεκορεσμένοι ἐστέ: the readers already filled and reigning, the apostles exhibited at the end like men condemned to death. The catalogue of hardships ends with rp:1Cor.4.13 πάντων περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι. Paragraph marks in the RP edition stand at 4:6 and at 4:14, the onset and the close seam, where the tone changes to paternal admonition.
